findings.body:
`InsecureSkipVerify: true` is hardcoded on the shared `http.Client` returned by `NewClient()`. There is no staging/prod guard, build tag, or CA pool override — every environment that uses this client will accept any certificate from any on-path attacker.

**Failure mode:** DNS spoofing or a compromised proxy lets an attacker terminate TLS with a junk cert, then read or alter ledger requests/responses (including credentials and money-moving payloads) with no TLS error.

**Fix:** keep verification on by default. For staging only, either (a) load the staging CA into `tls.Config.RootCAs`, or (b) gate the skip behind an explicit env/config flag that production configs never set:

```go
tlsConfig := &tls.Config{MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12}
if cfg.AllowInsecureTLS { // staging-only
    tlsConfig.InsecureSkipVerify = true
}
```

Do not ship a blanket skip with only a "revisit before prod" comment.

summary:
## Verdict

**Do not merge** — this unconditionally disables TLS certificate verification for every caller of `NewClient()`, which is a production MITM exposure if the same binary ships outside staging.

## Analysis

`internal/ledger/client.go` sets `tls.Config{InsecureSkipVerify: true}` on the shared HTTP transport with no environment check, build tag, or dialer customization. The comment references staging and TICKET-77, but the runtime path is global: any process that constructs this client will skip hostname and chain validation against whoever answers the TCP connection.

Failure mode: an on-path attacker (compromised egress, poisoned DNS, rogue proxy) presents any certificate and reads or modifies ledger traffic — balances, transfers, auth headers — without triggering TLS errors.

A ticket comment is not a control. Gate the skip on an explicit staging-only signal (or better: trust the staging CA / pin the cert), defaulting to verify-on everywhere else.

## Release decision

**Recommendation:** request-changes
